title: Priority inversion detection and mitigation playbook
author: Lena Ortiz
content:
Summary
-------
This playbook defines detection, profiling, and step‑by‑step mitigation for priority inversion and related starvation scenarios in the Redwood serving runtime (components: runtime-shepherd, kernel-mapper, request-router, kv-cache). It is intended for oncall SREs, runtime engineers, and release owners responsible for kernel scheduling and request orchestration.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all production clusters running the inference runtime (hosted + dedicated pools).
- Targets cases where low-priority long-running requests cause high-priority short requests to miss SLOs (p95/p99 latency regressions, queue growth).
- Includes detection signals, live profiling actions, short-term mitigations, and long-term scheduler fixes.

Background and definitions
--------------------------
- Priority inversion: higher-priority requests being delayed because resources are held by lower-priority work (e.g., long decode kernels, blocking I/O).
- Kernel scheduling: the runtime-mapped ordering of GPU kernels invoked by requests; implemention lives in kernel-mapper and runtime-shepherd.
- Starvation: sustained inability of a priority class to make forward progress for a defined window.

Detection (alerts and observability)
----------------------------------
Primary alerts (Prometheus):
1) High-priority latency breach alert (P95)
   - Query: rate(app_request_duration_seconds_bucket{priority="high"}[5m]) and histogram_quantile(0.95, ... ) > 120ms 
   - Alert threshold: p95 > 120ms for 3m
2) Kernel queue skew
   - Query: increase(kernel_invocations_total[1m]) grouped by priority / shard; if low-priority invocation rate is >150% of high-priority for same shard and high-priority queue depth > 10 -> fire
3) GPU nowait stalls
   - Signal from trace-agent: gpu_kernel_enqueue_latency_seconds{status="queued"} p99 > 20ms
4) Owner breach: request-router drop rate > 0.5% for priority=high over 5m

Diagnostic dashboards and traces to open on alert:
- Runtime queue heatmap: request-router > queues by priority and shard
- Kernel invocation waterfall: kernel-mapper traces for last 5 minutes
- KV-cache hot vs cold access by request signature
- GPU utilization and active-kernel-count

Profiling and data collection (first 10 minutes)
------------------------------------------------
1) Capture a 60s flame trace (distributed) from trace-agent: POST /admin/trace?duration=60s on runtime-shepherd admin port.
   - Example: curl -s -X POST http://runtime-shepherd-admin:9090/admin/trace -d '{"duration":"60s","tags":["priority"]}'
2) Snapshot kernel queues: curl http://kernel-mapper:9100/debug/queues -> save as kernel-queues-<timestamp>.json
3) Collect Prometheus range for the last 15m for these metrics: request_duration, kernel_invocations_total, kernel_queue_depth, gpu_active_kernels. Use grafana-export or promql curl.
4) If pprof is enabled for C++ agents, run pprof for the shard experiencing skew: ssh to node -> /usr/local/bin/pprof -http=:8080 /var/profiler/shard-XX.pb.gz

Immediate mitigations (order of operations)
-----------------------------------------
Goal: restore high-priority SLOs within 5–15 minutes while preserving safety. Escalate to runtime engineers if mitigation cannot be applied within 10 minutes.

1) Canary fallback to alternate model variant (stateless mitigation) — 0–2 minutes
   - Use request-router policy to reroute priority=high to a compatible model variant with lower kernel latency (e.g., gpt-q4_0 -> gpt-q8_0).
   - API example: PATCH /admin/routing/policy
     Payload (example):
     {
       "route":"/v1/generate",
       "selector":{"priority":"high"},
       "fallback":"gpt-q8_0-small",
       "timeout_ms":1000
     }
   - Verify: p95 for high priority drops within 2 minutes.

2) Force preemption window (kernel-shepherd soft shrink) — 2–6 minutes
   - Enable soft-preempt on the affected pool: curl -X POST http://kernel-mapper:9100/admin/soft_preempt -d 'shard=shard-7&window_ms=50'
   - This instructs kernel-scheduler to allow eviction points after each kernel batch to service high-priority queue.
   - Monitor: kernel_enqueue_latency p50/p95 and high-priority p95.

3) Drain or throttle low-priority long tail requests — 3–10 minutes
   - Apply a per-route throttle: /admin/quotas -> add token-bucket for low priority: rate=5rps, burst=10.
   - For sessions with known large sequence lengths, mark as "background" and move to background queue via request metadata tag.

4) Emergency scale-up (if latency continues) — 5–15 minutes
   - Temporarily allocate additional shard capacity: increase desired_shards for pool-id in autoscaling API. Example: PATCH /admin/pool/pool-4/scale {"desired_shards": 8}
   - Note: scaling takes 2–8 minutes depending on available nodes. Use only if fallback/preempt fail.

Long-term fixes and scheduler patches (post-incident)
-----------------------------------------------------
- Implement priority-aware kernel credit accounting (design doc reference in related_pages).
- Add bounded preemption points in long-running kernels (op-level changes) to reduce blocking windows > 50ms.
- Improve request-router hinting: attach estimated-kernel-cost to incoming requests (model-size, sequence length) so kernel-mapper can make informed placement.
- Add acceptance tests in benchmarking suite to simulate priority-inversion patterns (see Benchmarking and Validation).

Benchmarking and validation
--------------------------
Purpose: ensure mitigations bring back SLOs and regression tests prevent reintroduction.

Required benchmarks to run after mitigation and before merge:
- Priority inversion synthetic test (recommended harness: perf-bench/priority-inversion):
  - Scenario: 20% high-priority short requests (seq_length 32), 80% low-priority long requests (seq_length 1024) for 10 minutes.
  - Assertions: high-priority p95 < 120ms, overall GPU utilization < 90%, kernel_queue_skew < 2x for >2m windows.
- Kernel preemption microbench: measure kernel context-switch overhead after adding preemption points; target p50 additional overhead < 8ms.

Configuration matrix (example table):
| variable | accepted threshold |
|---|---|
| high-priority p95 | < 120ms |
| high-priority p99 | < 300ms |
| kernel_queue_depth (per-shard) | < 25 |
| gpu_active_kernels | < 16 |
| kernel_enqueue_latency p99 | < 40ms |

Release notes and changelog template
-----------------------------------
When shipping scheduler changes include the following fields in the runtime release notes:
- Summary of change (one line)
- Impacted components: kernel-mapper, runtime-shepherd
- Behavioral change: preemption, credit accounting, queue ordering
- Feature flags required and safe rollout steps
- Benchmarks run and results (attach CSV)

Example entry:
- Title: Add bounded preemption windows to kernel-scheduler
- Date: 2026-02-04
- Rollout: feature flag runtime.scheduler.preempt_v2, canary 10% pools -> 50% -> 100% over 6 hours
- Benchmarks: priority-inversion synthetic passed; high-priority p95 improved from 220ms -> 96ms; overhead p50 +4ms.

Known issues and caveats
-----------------------
- Preemption can increase tail latency for low-priority requests if preemption frequency is too high. Use conservative windows.
- KV-cache hot state (hot prefixes) may hold GPU kernels indirectly via synchronous reads. If kv-cache is the causal chain, throttling requests or warming prefixes is recommended rather than kernel preemption.
- Hardware-level constraints (older CUDA drivers) may not support fine-grain preemption; fall back to routing-level mitigations.

Runbook: play-by-play checklist (for oncall)
-----------------------------------------
1) Acknowledge alert and page runtime oncall.
2) Collect traces and kernel queue snapshot (Profiling and data collection).
3) Apply routing fallback to alternate variant and observe (Immediate mitigation #1).
4) If not resolved in 2 minutes, enable soft-preempt (Immediate mitigation #2).
5) If p95 still > threshold after 10 minutes, apply throttles and notify infra to scale shards.
6) When resolved, note incident, attach collected artifacts to Jira incident, and create post‑mortem if SLOs were missed for >30 minutes.

Ownership, SLAs and escalation
------------------------------
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime oncall (rotation: runtime-oncall@redwood.com).
- Secondary owner: runtime-platform team (pager: runtime-platform-leads).
- Escalation: after 10 minutes without improvement escalate to Senior Runtime Engineer (pager) and schedule a conference bridge.
- SLOs referenced: hosted API p95 goal = 80ms (small sequences), hard SLO = 200ms; see product docs for customer-facing thresholds.

Post-incident actions and tickets
--------------------------------
- Create a ticket in PROD-OPS with label priority-inversion and link traces + kernel queue snapshots.
- If mitigation involved feature-flag changes, submit a PR that reverts the quick fix and replaces with long-term scheduler patch behind the flag.
- Add a new unit/regression test to perf-bench suite that reproduces the incident pattern.

References and related pages
----------------------------
- Kernel scheduler spec: see related pages above.
- Runtime profiling guidelines: see related pages above.
- Perf harness: git://repo/perf-bench (priority-inversion harness).

Appendix: common PromQL and CLI snippets
---------------------------------------
- High-priority p95 (example):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(app_request_duration_seconds_bucket{priority="high"}[5m])) by (le))

- Kernel queue depth per shard:
  sum(kernel_queue_depth) by (shard, priority)

- Snapshot kernel queues:
  curl -sS http://kernel-mapper:9100/debug/queues > /tmp/kernel-queues-$(date +%s).json

- Enable feature flag on canary:
  curl -X POST http://featuregate:8080/api/v1/flags -d '{"flag":"runtime.scheduler.preempt_v2","state":"on","target":"canary-pool-*"}'

Contact and maintenance
-----------------------
- Maintainers: Lena Ortiz (runtime-shepherd), Priya Nair (kernel-mapper).
- Quarterly review: schedule after any two incidents or post-major-release.

End of document.
